9'

  • N: u kabta | dullani || i nišbir | nīr[ni]
  • T: and break our heavy work, our yoke!’
  • L: u ← u I “and, but, also”; kabta ← kabtu I “f. kabittu(m) heavy”; dullani ← dullu I “pl. m. & f. trouble”; i ← i I “let's”; nišbir ← šebēru I “to break”; nīr[ni] ← nīru I “yoke, crossbeam”
  • Note: [RN59aa: 170, 173] restore i ni-iš-h[u?-uṭ] from the verb šahāṭu “to cast off”. On the “sandwiching” of the verb between two accusatives, a well-attested device in Babylonian literature, see the remarks in [marquezrowe2016middle: 62].
BabMBSch1 o 9'. u₃ ka-ab-ta du-ul-la-ni i-ni-iš-bir₅ ni-ir-[ni]

10'

  • N: (w)ê | ša īšû || ilu | ṭēma
  • T: (Then) (W)e, the god who took the initiative,
  • L: (w)ê ← We I; ša ← ša I “who(m), which”; īšû ← išû I “to have (no pres., pret. īši, īšu”; ilu ← ilu I “pl. ilū, ilānu god, deity a or the god, also du.”; ṭēma ← ṭēmu I “pl. m. & f. (fore)thought, plan(ning)”
  • Note: On the name “(W)ê” of the god leader of the rebellion, previously interpreted by most scholars as Wê-ila or Aw-ila, see the commentary on this line in [marquezrowe2016middle: 62] (following [krebernik2002geschlachtet: 290]). [RN59aa: 173-74] read UN at the beginning. The epithet ša išû ilu ṭēma displays the same word order as in OB II 103, which shows that the two texts were closely related.
